questions.q: Why does this course exist at the end of a SQL Server-focused career path, per this lesson?
options: Real DBA roles at many companies expect one person to keep several different database engines healthy, not just SQL Server
SQL Server is being phased out in favor of these three platforms
This course actually re-teaches SQL Server using different syntax
There is no real reason — it's an arbitrary addition
questions.explain: A company that grew through acquisition or has varied legacy systems often needs one DBA covering multiple platforms, not a dedicated team per engine.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of something that transfers directly from SQL Server DBA experience, per this lesson?
options: Measuring before making a change, and the principle that an untested backup isn't a real backup
The exact RMAN command syntax for Oracle backups
SQL Server's specific buffer pool configuration option names
T-SQL's exact syntax for stored procedures
questions.explain: General relational database discipline transfers; SQL-Server-specific syntax and tooling do not.

questions.q: Why doesn't Oracle's SGA/PGA memory model simply map onto SQL Server's buffer pool with different terminology, per this lesson?
options: This course teaches each platform on its own terms because architecture details genuinely differ, not just naming
Oracle doesn't actually have a memory architecture
SGA and the buffer pool are identical concepts with identical behavior
SQL Server has no memory architecture to compare against
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly warns against treating platform-specific architecture as a simple relabeling of SQL Server concepts.

questions.q: Why does this course focus specifically on Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL?
options: Together with SQL Server, they cover the large majority of real-world relational database deployments a DBA is likely to encounter
They are the only three relational databases that exist
They were chosen at random
They are all owned by the same company
questions.explain: Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL each have a distinct, large real-world footprint (enterprise/legacy, web applications, and new open-source projects respectively).

questions.q: What approach does this course take when teaching a new platform, per its stated philosophy?
options: Teaching each platform on its own terms, the same discipline used when Azure Database Administrator taught cloud concepts rather than relabeling on-prem ones
Assuming every SQL Server concept has a directly equivalent feature with a different name
Skipping architecture entirely and only covering syntax
Treating all four platforms as functionally identical
questions.explain: This course explicitly avoids treating other platforms as SQL Server with translated syntax, consistent with this path's established teaching philosophy.
